newsitem.title: USA: Cheap corn, kill patterns push up U.S. hog weights.
newsitem.headline: Cheap corn, kill patterns push up U.S. hog weights.

text.p: Falling corn prices, improved hog producer profits and a change in weekly slaughter patterns is pushing market hog weights to record levels, analysts said.
"Since late summer, our hogs weights have gone straight up because corn prices have made a deep downward adjustment," said Chuck Levitt, analyst with Alaron Trading in Chicago.
On Wednesday the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported that the average weekly hog weight for the week ended October 26 in Iowa/Minnesota direct markets was 252.9 lbs, versus 251.3 lbs a year ago.
Last week's average weight surpassed the all-time record weight of 252.8 lbs, set in 1994 for that region, Levitt said.
"The bottom line is that hogs have gotten heavier, and I expect this year's weights will track 1994 levels or even eclipse them, Levitt said.

An industry-wide shift in slaughter patterns is also adding weight to some market hogs, analysts observed. Packers are now slaughtering more hogs during the five-day work week and far fewer on the weekend. That new schedule leaves some hogs with two extra days on feed.

"Last year on Saturday we used to kill 150,000 to 200,000 hogs, but lately we've been killing only 30,000 to 40,000," said Ron Plain, agricultural economist at the University of Missouri in Columbia, Mo.
Hogs that are not sold for the weekday slaughter and are held over for sale until Monday can gain as many as four additional pounds, Plain said.

Some market observers also attributed the weight gain trend to the fact that hogs are now being fed a diet consisting primarily of new-crop corn, which is believed to increase the rate of gain in most animals.
"It's a widespread belief among those in the industry that pigs just seem a little better in terms of weight gain when the new crop comes in," Plain said.
Plain said the improved weight gain on new-crop corn was probably due to the feed having a fresher taste, so it was therefore, more palatable to the hog.
Gerry Kuhl, extension feedlot specialist at Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kan., said that the biggest difference between the 1995 and 1996 corn crop was one of quality rather than freshness.

"The new corn crop is better in terms of quality, meaning yields and test weights, especially here in Kansas, were much better than last year, and that could have an effect on feed quality," Kuhl said.
Other factors contributing to this fall's record hog weights included mild weather throughout the Midwest during September and October, Plain said.
Although heavier weight hogs do increase available supplies of pork, if hog producers are making money, they are more likely to hold hogs for breeding, analysts said.
Hogs kept for expansion of the breeding herd take away from the total slaughter so it can be offsetting, Levitt said.
